newsitem.title: UK: N.Irish police criticised on plastic bullets.
newsitem.headline: N.Irish police criticised on plastic bullets.

text.p: The authority that monitors the operations of British police forces on Wednesday called on Northern Ireland's Royal Ulster Constabulary (RUC) to introduce new safeguards on its use of plastic bullets.

A report by the Inspector of Constabulary called on the RUC to think more carefully before issuing guns that fire plastic bullets, and to be more willing to refer allegations of their misuse to an independent commission.
Since 1972, 16 people have been killed in Northern Ireland in incidents involving plastic bullets, the last in 1989, and more than 500 have been injured.
The report said the use of the ammunition, known as plastic baton rounds, was justified in dealing with spontaneous outbreaks of disorder that often occur in the British-ruled province.
But it said the senior officer approving its use should always make a statement afterwards on his overall assessment of the threat to life posed by the incident.
The guns used by Northern Ireland police fire 38 mm rounds weighing 135 grams (4.7 ounces) that are designed to deliver at a distance the equivalent of a blow from a truncheon.

Introduced in the 1950s, they are potentially lethal but developments over the years to both the weapon and the round have been aimed at making their use as safe as possible, the Inspectorate of Constabulary report said.
But it said the issue of guns that fire plastic ammunition "should be governed by the formal assessment of intelligence and tension indicators".
"There is a risk that in those areas where baton guns are routinely issued, they will be treated as a piece of everyday equipment," it added.

The report said that unlike police forces in England and Wales, the RUC seldom referred incidents in which a policeman was accused of a criminal offence to the Independent Commission for Police Complaints.
"(The) Inspector suggests this should be considered as a reassurance to the public of the thoroughness and impartiality of the investigation," it said.

It also called for reports on the use of baton guns, submitted by the policemen who use them, to be more thoroughly analysed for pointers on how to improve training, deployment or operational guidelines.
